summary: This is a humorous April 1st memo that defines a MIME content type for transporting matter, specifically a sentient life form, across the network. It is a joke and not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: This is a joke paper about mailing a person through the Internet, like a letter. People wrote it for fun on April Fools' Day.

questions: can you send people through email
subtitle: A humorous MIME type for transporting sentient beings via email.

tldr.problem: Electronic mail can transport text, images and files, but the Internet standard MIME lacked a standard way to send actual people.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1437 defines a joke MIME type called matter-transport/sentient-life-form that theoretically describes a person as a 3D scan of molecules, one per location in a cubic grid.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st RFC and not a real protocol. It serves as humor while poking fun at how MIME extension works, and includes intentional caveats about the hazards of the approach.

today: RFC 1437 is an April 1st joke document and not a real protocol. It demonstrates the extensibility of MIME types while humorously pointing out the absurdity of trying to encode physical objects as email content. It remains a beloved example of RFC humor in the networking community.

sections.title: The Matter-Transport Content Type
sections.content:
This April 1st memo defines a fictional MIME content type intended to address a gap in electronic mail: the ability to send an entire sentient being (such as a human) as an email message. The RFC proposes a new content type called matter-transport/sentient-life-form that represents a three-dimensional rectangular solid containing a person, with height, width, depth, and resolution as parameters.

The data stream consists of a molecular description of each location within the cube using molecular formulas rendered in plain ASCII. The concept trades efficiency for simplicity, assuming that every location can be described by finding the single molecule closest to the center point at that location.
sections.eli5: The joke is that you could describe every atom in a person's body in a big 3D grid and send that grid through email. The RFC explains it very seriously, like a real protocol.

sections.title: Parameters and Data Format
sections.content: The Content-Type header includes four parameters: height, width and depth (in centimeters) describing the rectangular solid, and resolution (in Angstroms) specifying the quantization unit. For example, a 200 cm tall, 60 cm wide and deep person scanned at 10 Angstrom resolution would be specified as height=200; width=60; depth=60; resolution=10. Higher resolution produces better quality reproduction but creates much larger messages. The RFC suggests using content-transfer-encoding like quoted-printable to prevent line-wrapping systems from breaking up long molecular descriptions.
sections.eli5: You tell the email system the person's size and how detailed the scan is. Then you list every molecule in the right order, like a recipe for rebuilding them.

sections.title: Implementation Hazards
sections.content:
The RFC warns of serious implementation hazards with dry humor. It notes that NFS file systems with limited space can truncate messages unexpectedly, causing the unintended destruction of the person being transported. Byte-swapping on different systems can similarly corrupt the molecular data in unpleasant ways. The RFC sarcastically suggests that X.400 gateways, being incompatible with MIME, would likely reject the message with a cryptic error, leading recipients to delete it without realizing a human being was enclosed.

The memo also includes implementation guidance about handling the transmission safely, including the recommendation that one should "think hard" before reconstructing someone sent via this method.
sections.eli5: The authors warn that file systems might accidentally erase part of the person, or computers might rearrange the molecules in the wrong order. It's meant to be very funny and serious at the same time.

references.text: Borenstein, N. and N. Freed, "MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions): Mechanisms for Specifying and Describing the Format of Internet Message Bodies", RFC 1341, June 1992.
